| Indexed access | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ worst case |
| Traverse all elements | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Insert at known linked position | Requires shifting in general | $O(1)$ |
| Delete at known linked position | Requires shifting in general | $O(1)$ |
| Memory layout | Contiguous references | Separate node objects |
| Extra structural storage | Capacity overhead | Link references per node |
| Growth | May require resizing | Node-by-node allocation |

The asymptotic comparison is only part of the decision.

Array-based structures generally benefit from simpler representation, lower per-element structural overhead, and better memory locality. Linked structures require node allocation and additional references, and traversal follows objects that need not be contiguous in memory. Goodrich notes that even operations with the same asymptotic complexity can therefore have different constant factors, and that linked structures generally require more auxiliary storage per element. 

Linked structures, however, provide strong guarantees for structural updates. Once the relevant location is known, insertion or deletion can modify a constant number of links without shifting the remaining elements. They also avoid the occasional large resizing operation required by a dynamic array. 

The choice should therefore follow the operations required by the problem:

$$
\boxed{
\text{representation}
\rightarrow
\text{available operations}
\rightarrow
\text{computational costs}.
}
$$

This principle is more general than the comparison between arrays and linked lists. A data structure is useful because its representation makes some operations efficient while accepting costs elsewhere.

The next step is to separate this implementation question from the **abstract behaviour** expected by a data structure. Stacks, queues, and deques provide a clear example: each specifies how elements may enter and leave a collection, while several different internal representations can be used to implement that behaviour.

# Stacks, Queues, and Deques

A data structure can be described at different levels of abstraction.

At the implementation level, we may ask whether elements are stored in a dynamic array, a linked structure, or some other representation.

At the interface level, however, the important question is often different:

> Which operations are permitted, and what behaviour must those operations provide?

An **abstract data type** (ADT) defines a collection through its operations and their semantics without prescribing a particular internal representation.

This distinction can be expressed as:

$$
\boxed{
\text{ADT}
=
\text{behaviour and interface}
\neq
\text{implementation}.
}
$$

Stacks, queues, and deques illustrate this principle particularly clearly. All three maintain collections of elements, but they impose different rules on where elements may be inserted, accessed, and removed.

## Stacks

A **stack** stores elements according to the **last-in, first-out** principle:

$$
\text{LIFO}
=
\text{Last In, First Out}.
$$

The most recently inserted element is the first one that can be removed.

Conceptually:

```text
        top
         ↓
       ┌───┐
       │ D │  <- most recently inserted
       ├───┤
       │ C │
       ├───┤
       │ B │
       ├───┤
       │ A │  <- first inserted
       └───┘
```

If the insertion order is:

$$
A,B,C,D,
$$

the removal order is:

$$
D,C,B,A.
$$

The structure therefore exposes only one distinguished end: the **top**.

### The Stack ADT

The fundamental stack operations are:

```text
push(e)
pop()
top()
```

with supporting operations:

```text
is_empty()
len()
```

Their semantics are:

| Operation | Behaviour |
|:---:|:---:|
| `push(e)` | Add `e` to the top |
| `pop()` | Remove and return the top element |
| `top()` | Return the top element without removing it |
| `is_empty()` | Determine whether the stack contains no elements |
| `len()` | Return the number of elements |

Calling `pop()` or `top()` on an empty stack is an invalid operation and should be handled explicitly by the implementation.

Goodrich defines the stack ADT in precisely these LIFO terms, separating its permitted operations from the representation used to implement them. 

![A stack follows the last-in, first-out principle: elements are pushed onto and popped from the same end, called the top.](figures/stack-lifo.png){#fig-stack-lifo}

### Array-Based Stack

A Python list provides a natural representation for a stack if the end of the list is treated as the top.

The correspondence is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{push(e)}
&\rightarrow
\texttt{append(e)},
\\
\texttt{pop()}
&\rightarrow
\texttt{pop()},
\\
\texttt{top()}
&\rightarrow
\texttt{data[-1]}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For example:

```python
stack = []

stack.append("A")
stack.append("B")
stack.append("C")

value = stack.pop()
```

After the three insertions:

```text
[A, B, C]
       ↑
      top
```

and:

```python
stack.pop()
```

returns:

```text
C
```

without requiring any remaining element to be shifted.

Because the right end of a Python list corresponds to the end of its dynamic array, both insertion and removal there have amortized constant cost:

$$
\texttt{push}=O(1)
\quad\text{amortized},
$$

$$
\texttt{pop}=O(1)
\quad\text{amortized}.
$$

Accessing the top element is:

$$
O(1).
$$

A formal stack class can therefore be implemented as an **adapter** around a list: the list provides the storage mechanism while the stack interface exposes only the operations appropriate to the ADT.

This restriction is meaningful. A Python list also permits:

```python
data.insert(3, value)
data.pop(2)
data[5] = value
```

but those operations do not belong to the stack abstraction.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{using a list as storage}
\neq
\text{exposing the complete list interface}.
}
$$

Goodrich uses this array-based implementation to illustrate exactly this separation: Python's list already provides the necessary end operations, but it also exposes behaviours that a stack should not permit. 

### Linked Stack

The same ADT can instead be implemented with a singly linked list.

If the head represents the top:

$$
\texttt{top}
\longrightarrow
A
\longrightarrow
B
\longrightarrow
C,
$$

then `push` is insertion at the head and `pop` is deletion at the head.

From the previous section:

$$
T_{\text{insert-head}}(n)=O(1)
$$

and:

$$
T_{\text{delete-head}}(n)=O(1).
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{push}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{pop}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{top}
&=O(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Unlike the dynamic-array implementation, these update bounds are worst-case rather than amortized.

The observable stack behaviour is unchanged.

This demonstrates why ADT and implementation must be kept conceptually separate:

$$
\boxed{
\text{same abstraction}
\rightarrow
\text{different representations}.
}
$$

### Stacks and Reversal

The LIFO rule naturally reverses order.

Suppose elements are pushed in the sequence:

$$
x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{n-1}.
$$

The first element removed is:

$$
x_{n-1},
$$

followed by:

$$
x_{n-2},
$$

and eventually:

$$
x_0.
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{push in forward order}
+
\text{pop all elements}
=
\text{reverse order}.
}
$$

This simple property makes stacks useful whenever a computation must later revisit information in the opposite order from which it was encountered.

The recursion call stack studied earlier is an important example. Function calls accumulate in one order and complete in the reverse order.

### Matching Delimiters

Stacks also arise naturally when processing **nested structures**.

Consider:

```text
{[(a + b) * c] - d}
```

Each opening delimiter must eventually be matched by a corresponding closing delimiter, and nested delimiters must close in reverse order.

When an opening delimiter is encountered:

```text
(
[
{
```

it is pushed onto a stack.

When a closing delimiter is encountered:

```text
)
]
}
```

the top opening delimiter is popped and checked.

For:

```text
{ [ ( ) ] }
```

the opening delimiters arrive as:

$$
\{,\ [,\ (
$$

and must close as:

$$
),\ ],\ \}.
$$

That is exactly LIFO behaviour.

The algorithm can be expressed conceptually as:

```python
for token in expression:
    if token is opening:
        stack.push(token)

    elif token is closing:
        if stack.is_empty():
            return False

        if not matches(stack.pop(), token):
            return False

return stack.is_empty()
```

Each token is processed at most once and each stack operation is constant time, so for $n$ tokens:

$$
\boxed{
T(n)=O(n).
}
$$

The same structural principle can be used for nested markup such as paired HTML tags. Goodrich uses both delimiter matching and HTML tag matching as applications of the stack ADT. 

The important point is not the particular syntax of parentheses or tags. A stack is appropriate because **nested structures close in the reverse order in which they open**.

## Queues

A **queue** follows the **first-in, first-out** principle:

$$
\text{FIFO}
=
\text{First In, First Out}.
$$

Elements enter at the **back** and leave from the **front**.

If the insertion order is:

$$
A,B,C,D,
$$

the removal order is:

$$
A,B,C,D.
$$

Conceptually:

```text
front                         back
  ↓                             ↓
[A] -> [B] -> [C] -> [D]
```

The element that has waited longest is processed first.

### The Queue ADT

The fundamental operations are:

```text
enqueue(e)
dequeue()
first()
```

together with:

```text
is_empty()
len()
```

Their semantics are:

| Operation | Behaviour |
|:---:|:---:|
| `enqueue(e)` | Add `e` to the back |
| `dequeue()` | Remove and return the front element |
| `first()` | Return the front element without removing it |
| `is_empty()` | Determine whether the queue is empty |
| `len()` | Return the number of elements |

Goodrich defines the queue ADT through this FIFO discipline: insertion occurs at the back while access and deletion occur at the front. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

![A queue follows the first-in, first-out principle: elements enter at the back and leave from the front in their arrival order.](figures/queue-fifo.png){#fig-queue-fifo}

Queues appear whenever arrival order matters: task scheduling, request processing, buffering, breadth-first traversal, simulations, and producer-consumer systems all contain queue-like behaviour.

## Why `list.pop(0)` Is a Poor Queue

A direct implementation might use:

```python
queue = []

queue.append(value)
queue.pop(0)
```

The semantics appear correct:

- `append` inserts at the back;
- `pop(0)` removes from the front.

The representation, however, makes dequeue inefficient.

Suppose:

```text
[A, B, C, D]
```

is stored in a contiguous array and `A` is removed.

The remaining references must shift:

```text
before:
[A, B, C, D]

after removing A:
[_, B, C, D]

after shifting:
[B, C, D, _]
```

Approximately $n-1$ references may need to move.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\texttt{list.pop(0)}=\Theta(n).
}
$$

Goodrich identifies precisely this problem with the naïve array-based queue: although `append` is efficient, removing index zero forces all subsequent elements to shift. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

This is an important example of why selecting a data structure based only on convenient syntax can be misleading.

The question should instead be:

$$
\boxed{
\text{does the representation support the required operations efficiently?}
}
$$

## Circular Arrays

An efficient array-based queue avoids shifting elements.

Instead of requiring the front element to remain at index zero, the queue maintains the index of its current front.

Suppose an underlying array has capacity:

$$
N.
$$

If the front is at index:

$$
f,
$$

and the queue contains:

$$
s
$$

elements, the next free position at the back can be calculated as:

$$
\boxed{
(f+s)\bmod N.
}
$$ {#eq-circular-queue-back}

The modulo operation allows the logical queue to wrap around the end of the physical array.

For example, with capacity:

$$
N=8,
$$

a queue might occupy:

```text
index:    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
        +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
data:   | G | H |   |   |   | D | E | F |
        +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
                              ↑
                            front
```

The logical order is:

$$
D,E,F,G,H,
$$

even though the physical representation crosses the array boundary.

![A circular array decouples the logical order of a queue from physical array indices. Modular arithmetic allows the back of the queue to wrap from the final array position to index zero.](figures/circular-array-queue.png){#fig-circular-array-queue}

If the front element is removed, the new front index is:

$$
f_{\text{new}}
=
(f+1)\bmod N.
$$ {#eq-circular-queue-front}

No elements need to move.

Similarly, the next enqueue position is determined by modular arithmetic rather than by shifting the existing queue.

Goodrich develops the circular-array representation specifically to prevent the front from forcing repeated shifts or allowing unused space to accumulate indefinitely before the logical queue. 

### Queue Complexity

With a circular dynamic array:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{first}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{is\_empty}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{len}
&=O(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Insertion and deletion are also constant time except when resizing is required.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\texttt{enqueue}=O(1)
\text{ amortized},
}
$$

and:

$$
\boxed{
\texttt{dequeue}=O(1)
\text{ amortized}.
}
$$

The storage requirement for $n$ elements is:

$$
O(n).
$$

These are the bounds established by Goodrich for the array-based queue implementation. 

The analysis combines two ideas developed earlier:

$$
\text{circular indexing}
+
\text{dynamic-array resizing}.
$$

Modular arithmetic prevents shifting, while geometric resizing provides amortized constant-time growth.

## Linked Queues

A queue can also be implemented using a singly linked list.

Maintain:

```text
head -> front
tail -> back
```

For:

$$
A,B,C,
$$

the structure is:

```text
front                         back
  ↓                             ↓
[A] -> [B] -> [C] -> None
 ↑                 ↑
head              tail
```

To enqueue a new element $D$:

$$
\texttt{tail.next}
=
D,
$$

then:

$$
\texttt{tail}
=
D.
$$

To dequeue:

$$
\texttt{head}
=
\texttt{head.next}.
$$

Both require only a constant number of reference updates.

Thus:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{enqueue}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{dequeue}
&=O(1),
\\
\texttt{first}
&=O(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

These are worst-case bounds.

Again, the FIFO semantics are independent of the representation:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Queue ADT}
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{circular dynamic array},\\
\text{singly linked list}.
\end{cases}
}
$$

## Double-Ended Queues

A **double-ended queue**, or **deque**, generalises both stacks and queues by allowing insertion and deletion at either end.

Its fundamental update operations are:

```text
add_first(e)
add_last(e)
delete_first()
delete_last()
```

and its accessors include:

```text
first()
last()
is_empty()
len()
```

Goodrich defines the deque ADT symmetrically in exactly this way. 

Conceptually:

```text
       front                    back
         ↓                        ↓
     [ A ] <-> [ B ] <-> [ C ] <-> [ D ]
       ↑                           ↑
 insert/delete                 insert/delete
```

![A deque supports insertion and deletion at both ends, generalising the restricted access patterns of stacks and queues.](figures/deque-operations.png){#fig-deque-operations}

A deque can reproduce stack behaviour by using only one end:

$$
\text{push}
\rightarrow
\texttt{add\_last},
$$

$$
\text{pop}
\rightarrow
\texttt{delete\_last}.
$$

It can reproduce queue behaviour by inserting at one end and removing from the other:

$$
\text{enqueue}
\rightarrow
\texttt{add\_last},
$$

$$
\text{dequeue}
\rightarrow
\texttt{delete\_first}.
$$

Thus, in terms of permitted operations:

$$
\boxed{
\text{deque}
\supset
\text{stack and queue access patterns}.
}
$$

This does not mean that every application should use the most general possible interface. Restricting operations can express important invariants about how a collection is intended to be used.

## Implementing a Deque

A deque can be implemented with a circular dynamic array.

If the current front index is:

$$
f,
$$

moving one position backward can be calculated as:

$$
f_{\text{new}}
=
(f-1)\bmod N.
$$

The index of the current last element can be calculated from the front and current size:

$$
\boxed{
\text{back}
=
(f+s-1)\bmod N.
}
$$ {#eq-deque-back-index}

This allows both ends of the logical sequence to move through the physical array without shifting the existing elements. Goodrich describes the array-based deque as a direct extension of the circular-array queue, using the same front, size, and modular-indexing principles. 

A doubly linked list is another natural representation.

Because each node has both:

```text
prev
next
```

and the structure can maintain direct access to both boundaries, insertion and deletion at either end require only a constant number of link updates.

The two implementations therefore provide similar asymptotic interfaces:

| Operation | Circular dynamic array | Doubly linked list |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Add first | $O(1)$ amortized | $O(1)$ |
| Add last | $O(1)$ amortized | $O(1)$ |
| Delete first | $O(1)$ amortized | $O(1)$ |
| Delete last | $O(1)$ amortized | $O(1)$ |
| First | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Last | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Space | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |

Again, equal asymptotic bounds do not imply identical practical behaviour. Array-based implementations and linked implementations differ in memory layout, allocation patterns, resizing behaviour, and constant factors.

## Python and `collections.deque`

Python provides a general-purpose deque in the `collections` module:

```python
from collections import deque
```

Its interface naturally supports operations at both ends:

```python
data = deque()

data.append("A")
data.append("B")
data.appendleft("C")

data.pop()
data.popleft()
```

Conceptually:

```text
appendleft(e)  -> add at front
append(e)      -> add at back
popleft()      -> remove from front
pop()          -> remove from back
```

For queue-like code, this interface expresses the required behaviour more directly than repeatedly removing index zero from a Python list.

For example:

```python
from collections import deque

queue = deque()

queue.append("A")
queue.append("B")
queue.append("C")

first = queue.popleft()
```

The intent is immediately visible:

$$
\text{insert at back}
+
\text{remove from front}
\rightarrow
\text{FIFO queue}.
$$

Similarly, using:

```python
append()
pop()
```

on one end produces LIFO behaviour.

The broader lesson is not simply to prefer one Python class over another. It is to choose a structure whose supported operations correspond to the semantics and performance requirements of the problem.

## Choosing the Appropriate ADT

Stacks, queues, and deques differ primarily in the order in which elements become available.

A stack answers:

> Which element was inserted most recently?

A queue answers:

> Which element has been waiting longest?

A deque permits:

> Which element should be processed from either boundary?

Their access disciplines can be summarised as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Stack}
&\rightarrow
\text{LIFO},
\\
\text{Queue}
&\rightarrow
\text{FIFO},
\\
\text{Deque}
&\rightarrow
\text{both ends}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The choice of ADT should therefore precede the choice of representation.

First determine the required behaviour:

$$
\text{problem}
\rightarrow
\text{ADT}.
$$

Then determine how that abstraction should be implemented:

$$
\text{ADT}
\rightarrow
\text{representation}.
$$

Together:

$$
\boxed{
\text{problem}
\rightarrow
\text{abstraction}
\rightarrow
\text{representation}
\rightarrow
\text{complexity}.
}
$$

This sequence of decisions is one of the central ideas of data-structure design.

The same distinction becomes even more important for hierarchical data. A tree defines relationships between parents, children, ancestors, and descendants independently of whether those relationships are represented through linked nodes or an array. Trees therefore provide the next major step from linear collections to structured, non-linear data.

# Object-Oriented Programming

Python's object model provides more than built-in types such as integers, strings, lists, and dictionaries. Programmers can define new types whose objects combine state with operations that act on that state.

This capability is particularly important for data structures.

A stack, linked list, tree, priority queue, or graph is not merely a collection of functions operating on unrelated variables. Each represents a coherent abstraction with:

- internal state;
- structural invariants;
- permitted operations;
- defined behaviour.

Object-oriented programming provides one way to express that relationship directly.

A **class** defines the structure and behaviour associated with a type of object, while an **instance** is a particular object created according to that definition.

Conceptually:

$$
\boxed{
\text{class}
\rightarrow
\text{instances}
}
$$

and each instance combines:

$$
\boxed{
\text{state}
+
\text{behaviour}.
}
$$

This complements the distinction introduced earlier between an abstract data type and its implementation. An ADT specifies what behaviour a structure should provide; a class can provide a concrete Python implementation of that abstraction.

## Classes and Instances

Consider a simple two-dimensional point:

```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def distance_squared(self):
        return self.x**2 + self.y**2
```

Creating:

```python
p = Point(3, 4)
```

produces an instance of `Point`.

The instance maintains state:

```python
p.x
p.y
```

and provides behaviour:

```python
p.distance_squared()
```

The relationship can be represented conceptually as:

```text
          Point
            │
        instantiation
            │
            ▼
      ┌─────────────┐
 p -> │ x = 3       │
      │ y = 4       │
      │-------------│
      │ behaviour   │
      └─────────────┘
```

The object `p` has its own identity, type, and state, consistent with the Python object model developed earlier.

A second instance:

```python
q = Point(8, 2)
```

has the same type:

```python
type(p) is type(q)
```

but a different identity and potentially different state.

Thus:

$$
\text{same class}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{same object}.
$$

![A class defines a common structure and behaviour, while each instance is a distinct object with its own identity and instance state.](figures/class-instance-relationship.png){#fig-class-instance-relationship}

## Instance State and `self`

Inside an instance method, Python conventionally names the current instance:

```python
self
```

For:

```python
p.distance_squared()
```

the method operates on `p`.

Conceptually, the call corresponds to passing the instance to the method:

```python
Point.distance_squared(p)
```

This explains expressions such as:

```python
self.x
```

They mean:

> retrieve the attribute named `x` from the current instance.

The name `self` is not a special keyword. It is a strong Python convention that makes the role of the first instance-method parameter explicit.

Each instance can therefore maintain independent state:

```python
p = Point(3, 4)
q = Point(8, 2)

p.x = 10
```

Changing `p.x` does not change `q.x`, because `p` and `q` are different objects.

The state belongs to the instances, not to the local execution of the method.

## Construction and `__init__`

The method:

```python
__init__
```

is invoked as part of instance initialisation.

For:

```python
p = Point(3, 4)
```

Python creates a new instance and then uses:

```python
Point.__init__(p, 3, 4)
```

to initialise its state.

A typical constructor therefore establishes the object's initial **invariants**.

Suppose a bounded counter should never begin with a negative limit:

```python
class Counter:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        if limit < 0:
            raise ValueError("limit must be non-negative")

        self.limit = limit
        self.value = 0
```

The constructor prevents the object from beginning in an invalid state.

This is an important responsibility of class design:

$$
\boxed{
\text{construction}
\rightarrow
\text{establish valid state}.
}
$$

Later methods should preserve the relevant invariants as the object changes.

For a linked list, for example, those invariants concern relationships between nodes. For a heap, they will include structural and ordering properties. For a search tree, they will involve relationships between keys and subtrees.

## Instance and Class Attributes

Attributes do not all have the same ownership.

An **instance attribute** belongs to a particular instance:

```python
self.x = x
```

A **class attribute** belongs to the class object itself and is shared through the class namespace:

```python
class Point:
    dimensions = 2
```

Then:

```python
Point.dimensions
```

and normally:

```python
p.dimensions
```

both resolve to:

```text
2
```

unless the instance defines an attribute of the same name.

This distinction matters particularly for mutable objects.

Consider:

```python
class Container:
    values = []
```

The list is created as a class attribute. Instances that access it without shadowing the name therefore reach the same mutable object.

That may produce unintended shared state.

If each instance should own an independent list, it belongs in the instance initialisation:

```python
class Container:
    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []
```

This is another manifestation of the aliasing and mutability principles introduced earlier. Object-oriented syntax does not change Python's underlying reference semantics.

## Encapsulation

A class should expose the behaviour needed by its clients without requiring those clients to depend on unnecessary implementation details.

This principle is **encapsulation**.

Suppose a stack is implemented using:

```python
self._data = []
```

Client code should interact through operations such as:

```python
stack.push(value)
stack.pop()
stack.top()
```

rather than manipulating:

```python
stack._data
```

directly.

The distinction is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{public interface}
&\rightarrow
\text{what clients may rely on},
\\
\text{internal representation}
&\rightarrow
\text{how the behaviour is implemented}.
\end{aligned}
$$

If clients depend only on the public interface, the implementation may later change:

$$
\text{dynamic array}
\rightarrow
\text{linked representation}
$$

without requiring client code to change.

This is one of the principal benefits of encapsulation: implementation decisions can evolve while the abstraction remains stable. Goodrich emphasises this separation between public interfaces and internal details as a central object-oriented design principle. 

### Non-Public Members

Python does not enforce strict private access in the same manner as some languages.

By convention, a name beginning with a single underscore:

```python
_data
```

communicates that the member is intended for internal use.

For example:

```python
class Stack:
    def __init__(self):
        self._data = []
```

The underscore does not make `_data` inaccessible. It communicates an interface boundary:

> client code should not rely on this member.

Goodrich similarly describes the leading underscore as Python's convention for members that are considered non-public implementation details. 

Encapsulation in Python therefore depends substantially on disciplined interface design rather than absolute access restriction.

## Methods and Object Behaviour

Methods define operations associated with objects.

Consider:

```python
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._value = 0

    def increment(self):
        self._value += 1

    def value(self):
        return self._value
```

The object maintains state:

$$
\texttt{\_value}
$$

and exposes controlled operations over that state.

This is often preferable to allowing arbitrary external mutation because methods can preserve invariants.

For example:

```python
def increment(self):
    if self._value == self._limit:
        raise ValueError("counter limit reached")

    self._value += 1
```

can ensure:

$$
0\leq\texttt{\_value}\leq\texttt{\_limit}.
$$

The public method is therefore not merely syntactic packaging around an assignment. It defines a valid transition between object states.

This perspective becomes especially useful for mutable data structures:

$$
\boxed{
\text{method}
=
\text{controlled state transition}.
}
$$

## Special Methods

Python allows user-defined classes to participate in the language's standard syntax through **special methods**, conventionally written with double underscores.

Examples include:

```text
__len__
__getitem__
__setitem__
__contains__
__iter__
__eq__
__lt__
__str__
__repr__
```

These methods connect an object's implementation to Python syntax.

For example:

```python
len(obj)
```

can invoke:

```python
obj.__len__()
```

while:

```python
obj[j]
```

can invoke:

```python
obj.__getitem__(j)
```

and:

```python
x in obj
```

may be supported through:

```python
obj.__contains__(x)
```

or related iteration behaviour.

Thus Python's operators and built-in functions form part of an extensible object protocol.

The relationship is conceptually:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Python syntax}
\rightarrow
\text{special method protocol}
\rightarrow
\text{object behaviour}.
}
$$

Goodrich uses this mechanism extensively when constructing custom sequence-like classes and data structures. 

### Operator Overloading

Special methods also allow operators to acquire meanings appropriate to a user-defined type.

For example, a vector class might define:

```python
def __add__(self, other):
    ...
```

so that:

```python
u + v
```

produces vector addition.

This is **operator overloading**: the operator remains syntactically the same, but its behaviour depends on the types of its operands.

This should preserve the conceptual meaning expected from the abstraction. Defining:

```python
u + v
```

is useful when addition has a natural interpretation for the type. Overloading operators with surprising or unrelated behaviour weakens rather than improves the interface.

Special methods are therefore most useful when they make a custom object behave naturally within Python's existing protocols.

## Sequence Protocols

Consider a custom sequence class that supports:

```python
len(sequence)
```

and:

```python
sequence[j]
```

through:

```python
__len__()
```

and:

```python
__getitem__()
```

respectively.

Those two operations already establish a substantial part of sequence behaviour.

A simplified structure might be:

```python
class Sequence:
    def __len__(self):
        ...

    def __getitem__(self, j):
        ...
```

Higher-level operations can then be expressed in terms of those primitive behaviours.

For example, membership can conceptually be implemented as:

```python
def __contains__(self, value):
    for j in range(len(self)):
        if self[j] == value:
            return True

    return False
```

The implementation does not need to know whether the sequence internally uses:

- an array;
- a linked structure;
- a mathematical formula;
- some other representation.

It relies only on the public behaviours:

$$
\texttt{len(self)}
$$

and:

$$
\texttt{self[j]}.
$$

This is a powerful abstraction principle:

$$
\boxed{
\text{higher-level behaviour can be constructed from a small primitive interface}.
}
$$

Goodrich uses the `Sequence` abstraction to demonstrate exactly this relationship: operations such as membership, `index`, and `count` can be defined generically once length and indexed access are supplied. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

## Iteration

Python's iteration model is also protocol-based.

When evaluating:

```python
for value in collection:
    process(value)
```

Python needs a mechanism for obtaining elements successively from `collection`.

An **iterator** is an object that represents the state of such a traversal.

Conceptually:

$$
\text{iterable}
\rightarrow
\text{iterator}
\rightarrow
x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots
$$

Python's iterator protocol centres on:

```python
__iter__()
```

and:

```python
__next__()
```

Calling:

```python
iter(collection)
```

requests an iterator.

Repeated calls to:

```python
next(iterator)
```

produce successive values until the iterator signals that no values remain.

This separates two concepts:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{iterable}
&\rightarrow
\text{object that can produce an iterator},
\\
\text{iterator}
&\rightarrow
\text{object representing one traversal}.
\end{aligned}
$$

![An iterable produces an iterator, which maintains traversal state and returns successive elements until the sequence is exhausted.](figures/python-iterator-protocol.png){#fig-python-iterator-protocol}

The distinction allows multiple independent traversals over the same collection because each iterator can maintain its own traversal state.

Iteration is therefore not merely syntax associated with `for`. It is an interface between an algorithm and a collection.

An algorithm can request:

> give me the next element

without knowing how the collection stores that element internally.

This is another example of abstraction through protocol.

## Generators

Python provides **generators** as a concise way to implement iterative behaviour.

A function containing:

```python
yield
```

does not behave like an ordinary function that computes a single result and terminates. Instead, its execution can suspend while preserving local state and later resume from that point.

For example:

```python
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
```

Using:

```python
for value in countdown(3):
    print(value)
```

produces:

```text
3
2
1
```

without first constructing:

```python
[3, 2, 1]
```

as a complete collection.

The generator therefore separates:

$$
\text{producing values}
$$

from:

$$
\text{storing all values simultaneously}.
$$

For a sequence of $n$ generated values, eager materialisation may require:

$$
O(n)
$$

additional storage.

A generator can often retain only the state needed to produce the next value:

$$
O(1)
$$

additional state for simple generators such as the example above.

The precise space requirement depends on the generator's internal state, but the broader principle is important:

$$
\boxed{
\text{iteration does not require materialising an entire collection}.
}
$$

This becomes valuable when processing large data streams, traversing structures, or constructing algorithmic pipelines.

## Inheritance

A class can reuse and specialise behaviour defined by another class through **inheritance**.

Suppose:

```python
class Base:
    ...
```

and:

```python
class Derived(Base):
    ...
```

Then `Derived` is a subclass of `Base`, while `Base` is its superclass.

Conceptually:

$$
\text{Base}
\longrightarrow
\text{Derived}.
$$

The subclass inherits available behaviour from the superclass and may:

- use inherited methods unchanged;
- add new behaviour;
- override inherited behaviour.

Goodrich describes inheritance in terms of **specialisation** and **extension**: a subclass may refine existing behaviour while also introducing capabilities not present in its superclass. 

### Extending a Class

Suppose a base class defines:

```python
class Collection:
    def __init__(self):
        self._size = 0

    def __len__(self):
        return self._size
```

A subclass can inherit the length behaviour and add operations specific to its abstraction.

The inherited implementation need not be rewritten.

This can reduce duplication when several related classes genuinely share behaviour and invariants.

### Overriding

A subclass may provide a new implementation of an inherited method.

For example:

```python
class BaseCollection:
    def describe(self):
        return "collection"


class SortedCollection(BaseCollection):
    def describe(self):
        return "sorted collection"
```

Calling:

```python
obj.describe()
```

uses the implementation appropriate to the actual object.

Overriding allows a subclass to specialise inherited behaviour while retaining the broader interface.

Goodrich also notes that overriding can improve efficiency. A generic sequence might implement membership through linear traversal, while a specialised representation may be able to determine membership more efficiently. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

This connects inheritance directly to algorithmic design:

$$
\boxed{
\text{same interface}
+
\text{specialised representation}
\rightarrow
\text{specialised algorithm}.
}
$$

## `super()`

A subclass sometimes needs to extend rather than replace the initialisation or behaviour of its superclass.

Python provides:

```python
super()
```

for cooperative access to inherited behaviour.

For example:

```python
class NamedPoint(Point):
    def __init__(self, x, y, name):
        super().__init__(x, y)
        self.name = name
```

The superclass establishes:

```python
x
y
```

while the subclass adds:

```python
name
```

This avoids duplicating the superclass initialisation logic.

The design principle is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{reuse established behaviour rather than reproduce it}.
}
$$

Inheritance is most valuable when the subclass genuinely satisfies the conceptual relationship represented by the superclass, rather than merely sharing a few lines of code.

## Polymorphism

**Polymorphism** allows the same operation to be applied to objects of different concrete types when those objects support the required behaviour.

Suppose an algorithm requires only:

```python
len(data)
```

and iteration over `data`.

The algorithm need not necessarily know whether `data` is:

```text
list
tuple
str
custom sequence
```

If each object supports the required protocol, the same algorithm can operate on all of them.

This can be expressed as:

$$
\boxed{
\text{algorithm depends on behaviour}
\quad
\text{rather than concrete representation}.
}
$$

In Python, polymorphism frequently arises without an explicit inheritance relationship.

A function such as:

```python
def first_item(data):
    return data[0]
```

can operate on any object that meaningfully supports indexed access.

The function asks for a capability:

```text
getitem
```

rather than requiring one particular concrete class.

This style is commonly described as **duck typing**.

Goodrich contrasts this implicit behavioural approach with formal abstract base classes: Python often allows an abstraction to be used simply because an object supports the expected operations, with incompatibilities appearing at runtime if those expectations are not satisfied. 

## Abstract Base Classes

Duck typing is flexible, but some designs benefit from explicitly defining a common interface.

An **abstract base class** (ABC) describes behaviour expected from concrete subclasses and may prevent direct instantiation until required operations have been implemented.

Conceptually:

$$
\text{Abstract Interface}
\longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{Concrete Implementation A},\\
\text{Concrete Implementation B},\\
\text{Concrete Implementation C}.
\end{cases}
$$

![An abstract base class defines a common interface while multiple concrete subclasses provide different implementations of that abstraction.](figures/abstract-base-class.png){#fig-abstract-base-class}

For example, a sequence abstraction might require concrete implementations of:

```text
__len__()
__getitem__()
```

while providing generic implementations of:

```text
__contains__()
index()
count()
```

in terms of those primitives.

This is an example of the **template method** pattern:

$$
\boxed{
\text{generic algorithm}
+
\text{required primitive operations}
=
\text{reusable behaviour}.
}
$$

Goodrich uses the sequence abstraction as the central example: once a subclass supplies concrete length and indexed-access operations, inherited higher-level sequence behaviours become well defined. 

Python's `abc` facilities can formally declare such requirements, while the standard library provides established abstract collection interfaces.

The conceptual value is larger than the syntax. An ABC separates:

$$
\text{what a family of objects must support}
$$

from:

$$
\text{how each concrete object provides it}.
$$

## Composition and Inheritance

Inheritance is not the only way to construct an abstraction from existing components.

**Composition** builds an object by containing and coordinating other objects.

The stack implementation introduced earlier is a simple example:

```python
class Stack:
    def __init__(self):
        self._data = []
```

A stack **has a** list as part of its representation:

$$
\text{Stack}
\rightarrow
\text{contains List}.
$$

It is not conceptually a specialised kind of list.

Therefore composition is more appropriate than:

```python
class Stack(list):
    ...
```

The distinction is commonly expressed as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{inheritance}
&\rightarrow
\text{is-a relationship},
\\
\text{composition}
&\rightarrow
\text{has-a relationship}.
\end{aligned}
$$

A stack implemented with a list has a storage component whose interface is deliberately hidden behind the stack abstraction.

Composition also allows the representation to change independently:

$$
\text{list-backed stack}
\rightarrow
\text{linked stack}
$$

while preserving the same public stack interface.

This reinforces the principle developed throughout these notes:

$$
\boxed{
\text{public abstraction should not unnecessarily expose internal representation}.
}
$$

## Designing Classes Around Responsibilities

A class should represent a coherent responsibility rather than simply collect related variables and functions.

A useful design process asks:

> What state does this object own?

> What invariants must it preserve?

> What operations should clients be allowed to perform?

> Which details should remain internal?

Goodrich frames object-oriented design similarly in terms of responsibilities, independence, and clearly defined behaviours. 

For a data structure, this produces a progression such as:

$$
\text{required operations}
\rightarrow
\text{public interface}
\rightarrow
\text{representation}
\rightarrow
\text{invariants}
\rightarrow
\text{implementation}.
$$

This is more robust than beginning with a collection of attributes and adding methods opportunistically.

### Prefer Small Public Interfaces

A class should expose the operations required by its abstraction, not every operation that its internal representation happens to support.

If a stack uses a list internally, exposing arbitrary indexed assignment would weaken the stack abstraction.

If a tree stores linked nodes internally, allowing external code to modify arbitrary parent and child references could violate tree invariants.

A narrow interface makes invalid states harder to construct and implementation changes easier to manage.

### Preserve Invariants Locally

Operations that modify a structure should leave it in a valid state.

For a doubly linked list, for example:

$$
x.next=y
$$

should correspond consistently with:

$$
y.prev=x.
$$

The class should centralise the code responsible for maintaining those relationships rather than requiring client code to manipulate links directly.

Encapsulation therefore has an algorithmic role as well as a software-engineering role: it protects the assumptions on which data-structure operations depend.

## Object-Oriented Design and Data Structures

The object-oriented mechanisms introduced here are not independent features to be used merely because Python provides them.

They support a hierarchy of abstraction:

$$
\boxed{
\text{problem}
\rightarrow
\text{ADT}
\rightarrow
\text{public interface}
\rightarrow
\text{class}
\rightarrow
\text{internal representation}.
}
$$

At each level, unnecessary details from the level below can be hidden.

For a stack:

$$
\text{LIFO abstraction}
\rightarrow
\texttt{push/pop/top}
\rightarrow
\text{Stack class}
\rightarrow
\text{dynamic array or linked nodes}.
$$

For a sequence:

$$
\text{ordered collection}
\rightarrow
\texttt{len/index/iteration}
\rightarrow
\text{sequence implementation}
\rightarrow
\text{chosen storage representation}.
$$

Inheritance can share behaviour across genuinely related abstractions. Composition can build structures from independent components. Special methods allow custom types to participate naturally in Python's protocols. Iterators separate traversal from representation. Abstract interfaces allow algorithms to depend on capabilities rather than concrete implementations.

These mechanisms become especially valuable as data structures become more complex.

The linear structures considered so far organise elements along a single sequence. The next structures introduce hierarchy. **Trees** represent elements through parent-child relationships, and their recursive structure will bring together many of the ideas developed so far: nodes and references, recursion, iteration, abstract interfaces, inheritance, and algorithmic complexity.
